summary: This experimental document describes a resolver discovery service for URNs implemented with a new DNS record, NAPTR, which gives rules for mapping parts of URIs to domain names. It was replaced by RFCs 3401 through 3404.

eli5.summary: A signpost that tells you which office to visit to look up a name.

questions: what is urn resolution using dns
subtitle: An experimental way to use DNS records to find the server that can resolve a URN or URL.

tldr.problem: URLs name a particular path on a particular host, so they break when the file moves or is copied elsewhere. Persistent names (URNs) need some way to find a resolver without the name saying where it lives.
tldr.mechanism: A new DNS record type, NAPTR, holds rewrite rules. The client turns the start of a URI into a domain name ending in .urn.net, follows the NAPTR rules to a final domain name, then looks up SRV or A records to find resolver hosts.
tldr.outcome: The document was published as Experimental to gain operational experience. It has been replaced by RFCs 3401, 3402, 3403 and 3404.

today: RFC 2168 is Experimental and has been replaced by RFC 3401, RFC 3402, RFC 3403 and RFC 3404. It was also updated by RFC 2915.

sections.title: Why URLs Needed Help
sections.content:
URLs are the foundation of the World Wide Web, but the RFC calls them brittle: a URL usually identifies one path to a file on one host. There is no graceful way to change the path or host later, or to replicate the resource for better network use and fault tolerance.

Uniform Resource Names (URNs) were proposed as persistent, location-independent identifiers. In the compromise known as the Knoxville framework, the resolution system must be separate from the way names are assigned. That raises one problem: how do you resolve a name that cannot tell you where its resolver is?

The answer here is a resolver discovery service. DNS is widely deployed, but the RFC says it should not hold information about each individual resource: it was never meant for that many records, its record size is too small for catalog information, and domain names are not suitable as URNs. So DNS is used only to locate resolvers, which can then answer for individual resources.
sections.eli5: A name on its own does not say where to find the thing. So we first ask a phone book which helper knows about that kind of name, and then ask the helper.

sections.title: How NAPTR Rewriting Works
sections.content:
The client takes the colon-delimited prefix of the URI (for a URN, the namespace identifier after urn:), appends .urn.net and asks DNS for NAPTR (Naming Authority PoinTeR) records at that name. The rules in the records rewrite the URI into the next domain name to query. The client does all the substitutions and lookups; DNS servers do not.

A key design choice keeps rule sets understandable: the rules are always applied to the original URI, never to the output of previous rules.

The last NAPTR in a chain is called terminal. Its flags say what to look up next: SRV records, A records, or a protocol-specific step. The SRV records then name the hosts that can do the resolving, with a port. The RFC recommends that DNS servers send SRV and A records as additional information with NAPTR answers, so that with a long TTL the average number of DNS probes for resolving a URN would approach one.

The authors expect the replacement field to be enough for most cases. Regular expressions are needed mainly when parts of a namespace are delegated to different resolvers.
sections.eli5: Each signpost tells you the next place to look. When you reach a sign that says 'stop, ask here', you look up the actual helpers and pick one.

sections.title: The NAPTR Record Fields
sections.content:
The DNS type code for NAPTR is 35. Besides the usual domain, TTL and class, the record has six fields.

  • order: a 16-bit integer. Records are processed from low to high, and once a record matches, the client MUST NOT consider records with a higher order. This is what makes delegation work.
  • preference: a 16-bit integer ordering records with equal order, low first, similar to an MX preference.
  • flags: single characters from [A-Z0-9], case-insensitive. A client that sees an unknown flag MUST ignore that record and move on, even before checking order.
  • service: an optional protocol followed by zero or more + resolution services. A protocol MUST be given if the record is terminal.
  • regexp: a substitution expression applied to the original URI.
  • replacement: the next name to query, used when the next name is fixed.

Resolution services include N2L (URN to URL), N2R (URN to the resource), N2C (URN to a collection of descriptive information) and L2R (URL to the resource). The protocols known at the time were rcds, thttp, hdl, rwhois and z3950.
sections.eli5: Each signpost has a priority number, a note saying what kind of help is offered, and either a fixed address or a rule for building the address.

sections.title: The Substitution Expression
sections.content:
The regexp field is a sed-like substitution expression, but real sed expressions are not used. It MUST follow a grammar: a delimiter character, a POSIX extended regular expression, the replacement, the delimiter again, and an optional i flag for case-insensitive matching. The first character is the delimiter, and there must be exactly three non-escaped delimiters. Digits MUST NOT be used as delimiters.

The replacement can include backreferences \1 to \9, which are filled from the parenthesised groups of the expression. The result MUST be a legal DNS host name, and clients SHOULD check that before querying it.

Administrators are warned that every backslash must be typed twice in a zone file to appear once in a query response, and that the shell can also eat backslashes. Rules must operate on the canonical URN form, where unusual characters are %-encoded, so rules for international characters would be nearly impossible to read or write by hand.
sections.eli5: A rewrite rule is like a find-and-replace that turns a long name into the short address of the next office to ask. Writing these rules is fiddly, so the RFC warns you to be careful.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples. In the first, the hypothetical URN urn:duns:002372413:annual-report-1997 leads to NAPTR records at duns.urn.net. They offer three protocols in preference order: dunslink, then RCDS, then HTTP. All carry the s flag, so the next step is an SRV lookup, which returns three candidate hosts and port 1000.

In the second, a MIME Content-Id URN urn:cid:199606121851.1@mordred.gatech.edu uses a regexp at cid.urn.net to extract gatech.edu. That name has its own NAPTR records, which are terminal.

The third shows that NAPTR can also front existing URLs. For http://www.foo.com/software/latest-beta.exe, a rule at http.urn.net extracts www.foo.com, whose records point to mirror sites chosen by the publisher.
sections.eli5: The examples show the signpost game with real-looking names: a business number, an email message ID and a web address that has copies on several computers.

sections.title: Caveats and Security
sections.content:
The RFC explains why it is Experimental rather than standards-track: URN resolution was new to the IETF, the approach inherits DNS security and administration concerns, it could noticeably affect DNS, the regular-expression rules are hard for people to get right, and the requirements document for URN resolution services was not finished.

On security, using urn.net as the registry is open to denial-of-service and DNS spoofing attacks. NAPTR records were expected to be signed with SIG records once DNSSEC work was deployed. Rewrite rules expose other namespaces to the same attacks as ordinary domain names. Regular expressions should be checked for sanity, not blindly passed to something like PERL. How a client then talks to the resolver is out of scope and has its own security considerations.
sections.eli5: Because everything goes through the DNS phone book, someone could try to trick it or overload it. The authors also said it was only a trial so they could learn from real use.
